He tells his readers to picture Atlantis before the flood, a northern kingdom ruled by a caste called the Azen.

When the island sank, its survivors scattered in every direction, carrying their memories with them.

In the north, those memories became the legends of Odin's Hall. Far the south, Hebrew chroniclers retold the same story in new language, turning the twelve Azen into the twelve tribes and the stronghold of Asgard into Zion.

To support this idea, Wieland lays out what he calls fingerprints. First, he notes that Atlantis, Asgard and the Israelite camp all show the same governmental outline, one supreme ruler presiding over exactly twelve territorial chiefs.

Second, he claims the Azen families bore animal totems. Wolf, eagle, lamb, that match the heraldic beasts later listed by rabbinic writers for Israel's tribal standards.

He argues that those twelve Azen symbols were projected onto the sky as the zodiac, which is why in his view, the water bearer should be read not as an oriental figure, but as an Atlantean sea lord.

By the time he finishes, Odin's council and Jacob's sons stand merged into a single Atlantean genealogy.

For Wieland, this is proof that the Bible itself is a northern saga written in a foreign script and that the bloodline of Israel is quite literally Germanic.

Rosenberg describes early Aryan history as one continuous Nordic wave. It begins, he writes, with the legendary march of the Atlanteans across North Africa, Persia and India, followed by the Dorians, Macedonians and Italic tribes, and the diffusion of the Germanic folkish migration, culminating in the colonisation of the world by the Germanic West.

In Persia, that wave first appears as a ruling elite and then as a religious reform.

The Behistun text is a huge trilingual proclamation carved by order of King Darius I of Persia on a cliff at Behistun, modern Bisotun in western Iran.

It was engraved around 520 BC, some 100 metres above ground level, and contains the same message in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian cuneiform.

It is Darius proclaiming, I Darius the great king of the Aryan race, while Zoroaster calls Persians back to Aryan blood in the struggle between Ahura Mazda and Ahriman.

Crossing the Hindu Kush, the migrants enter India as Indo-Aryans. Rosenberg says they created a gulf between themselves as conquerors and the Black Brown natives, erected the Varna caste wall to keep their blood separate, and produced the earliest Vedic hymns.

The Rig Veda is a collection of 1028 Sanskrit hymns arranged in 10 bucks mandalas.

These have been dated to roughly 1500 to 1200 BC, not long after Indo-Aryan speakers entered northwest India.

The hymns praise sky and ritual deities such as Indra, the Storm Warrior, and include famous speculative poems like the Nasadiyya Sukta on the origins of the universe.

They were passed on orally with great precision for centuries before later Vedas and commentaries were added.

Turning west, Nordic clans push into Greece. Wave upon wave came from the Danube Valley.

The ancient Mycenaean culture of the Achaeans was predominantly Nordic, and later Dorian invaders overthrow King Minos, building classical Hellas on aristocratic ideas that forbids racial mixing.

From Greece, the migration stream moves on to Italy. Rosenberg says Rome too was established by a Nordic folkish wave that poured into the fertile valleys to the south of the Alps.

It broke the dominion of the Etruscans, that mysterious and alien Near Eastern people.

Presumably this wave blended with the still pure indigenous tribes of the Mediterranean race, producing a hybrid character of the greatest toughness and tenacity.

One that combined a lively intellect with the iron energy of masters, farmers and heroes.

In Rosenberg's reading, Early Rome held its power only while the Nordic Mediterranean mix remained strong.

Later intermarriage with Eastern peoples, he argues, sapped the city's original vitality and left it vulnerable to the Oriental menace it had once resisted.

The alliance is possible, but only if both nations defend their shared Nordic stock.

Racial anthropologist Hans F. K. Gunther filled in the map behind that warning. He judged the lowland English to be the most thoroughly Nordic of the British peoples, but warned that the British Isles show a gradation in the decline of Nordic blood.

Wales, Dorset, Devon and West Somerset and North West Ireland display an Alpine Nordic Mediterranean mixture.

The inland counties of Northampton, Huntington, Bedford, Buckingham and Hertford are dark.

In NS thinking then, Britain belonged to the wider Germanic family yet showed more Celtic Mediterranean admixture, especially along the Welsh, Cornish and Irish fringes than the German heartland.

That difference, they claimed, explained why Germany should take the ideological lead.

Its larger rural population and stricter racial vigilance had preserved a higher proportion of the original Nordic blood, whereas Britain tilted toward maritime trade and empire risked drifting further from the shared northern heritage it was still invited to defend.

Rosenberg's migration map, Persia to India, then Greece, Italy and finally Britain is the best known Nordic wave, but it was never the only one.

Take the Swedish adoption twin study of aging, Sätse for instance. In the early 1990s Plomin and his colleagues studied older twins, some reared apart, some together, to investigate the causes of stressful life events.

Using the social readjustment rating scale, which includes real-world events like illness, job loss and the death of a spouse, they found that identical twins were twice as similar as fraternal twins in how they responded to these events, even if raised in entirely different households.

This pointed to a heritability of roughly 30 percent for what had always been assumed to be purely environmental events.

In other words, how we perceive and respond to life stress is significantly shaped by our genes.

Another case, divorce. In a twin study of over 1,500 adult sibling pairs, concordance rates for divorce were 55 percent for identical twins and 16 percent for fraternal twins, suggesting an underlying genetic influence.

This definitely wasn't a fluke. A later adoption study in Sweden followed 20,000 adopted individuals and found that their likelihood of divorce was more strongly connected to whether their biological parents had divorced than whether their adoptive parents had.

This clearly wasn't environmental factors, but their DNA. And our ancestors already knew.

Published in the International Journal for Equity in Health, the research focused on 117 Alaska Native individuals from two regions examining how experiences of historical loss and trauma are associated with DNA methylation patterns, specific chemical modifications that can influence gene expression.

Participants who strongly identified with their Alaska Native heritage and actively engaged in tribal and cultural practices reported better overall wellbeing.

Cultural and tribal belonging isn't optional, it's essential. It forms a buffer against fragmentation, alienation and decay.

A groundbreaking study led by Professor Reepan Malhi from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign in collaboration with Alaska Native communities has provided compelling evidence linking historical trauma to epigenetic changes and by extension to the biological roots of tribal identity.

Published in the International Journal for Equity and Health, the research focused on 117 Alaska Native individuals from two regions examining how experiences of historical loss and trauma are associated with DNA methylation patterns, specific chemical modifications that can influence gene expression.

The study found that participants who reported more intense symptoms of distress when reflecting on historical traumas such as colonization, forced relocation and cultural suppression exhibited distinct epigenetic markers at five CPG sites.

This shows that the psychological impacts of collective trauma become biologically embedded. needed, reinforcing that the experience of being torn from one's tribe, one's ancestral structure has measurable generational consequences.

Importantly, the research also highlighted the protective role of tribal identity and continuity.

Participants, who strongly identified with their Alaska native heritage and actively engaged in tribal and cultural practices, reported better overall wellbeing.

These results show something that nationalists and traditionalists have long understood.

Cultural and tribal belonging isn't optional, it's essential. It forms a buffer against fragmentation, alienation and decay.

This study adds to a growing body of evidence indicating that the legacy of historical trauma can have lasting biological effects and that the healing power of tribal cohesion, ritual and shared ancestry is symbolic and physiological.

It affirms that human beings are not meant to live as atomised individuals, we are tribal to our core.

And when that tribal structure is violated, it leaves scars deep in the genome.
